                 Abstract
                 Characterising the mechanical behaviour of porous subsurface reservoirs is essential for avoiding hazards
                 such as wellbore failure, fault reactivation, seal leakage and gas migration during CO2 storage. Reactivation
                 of faults is a particular concern when CO2 is injected into reservoirs that contain them. To address this, a
                 geomechanical model (GM) was built for the South-West Hub (SWH) Carbon Capture and Storage (CCS)
                 reservoir, drawing on data from the Harvey field wellbores in Western Australia. The 3D GM combined
                 a geological model with seismic data, dynamic-simulation output, and one-dimensional mechanical-earth
                 models. A 4D finite-element model was then used to capture how CO2 injection alters stress and deformation
                 within the storage formation, and to characterise the failure behaviour and performance of the reservoir as
                 injection proceeds. Effective-stress azimuth and magnitude were tracked throughout the injection period.
                 Estimated magnitudes for Sv, SH and Sh across the study area show SH ranging from 22 to 75 MPa and Sh
                 from 21 to 72 MPa.
                    Fault strain responses are compared across a set of injection scenarios. Five separate reservoir-pressure
                 and saturation profiles were used to calibrate the 3D model, which was then re-run repeatedly to refine
                 the stress model against available leak-off test (LOT) data. The calibrated model was subsequently used
                 to run fault-stability analyses and identify which faults are most prone to reactivation under the pore-
                 pressure changes generated by ongoing CO2 injection. Over 30 faults intersecting the reservoir were mapped,
                 mostly trending N-S in keeping with the dominant regional fault orientation. Combining the dynamic and
                 geomechanical results indicates that CO2 injection does not pose a substantial fault-failure risk for the SWH
                 reservoir. This assessment describes the isothermal, pressure-driven response: thermal stresses arising from
                 injecting CO2 colder than the formation are not represented and may be significant near the injection wells.
                 Keywords: 4D Finite-element analysis, coupled geomechanical modeling, fault reactivation risk, in-situ
                 stresses, CO2 sequestration.

                 Introduction
                 Global warming is a major challenge that will require sustained effort over coming decades to address. In
                 response, researchers have pursued ways to cut CO2 emissions from fossil-fuel use and to limit the longer-
                 term consequences of a warming climate (Bachu 2000; Preston and Jones 2006; Bhattacharyya et al., 2021).
                 Among the key technologies for doing so is capturing surplus CO2 and injecting it into underground porous
                 rock formations, such as depleted petroleum reservoirs (Herzog et al., 1998; Bachu and Adams., 2003;
                 Matter and Takahashi., 2007; Steefel et al., 2013; Jia et al., 2019; Gin et al., 2021).
                    Certain Australian sub-surface reservoirs, among them the Harvey Ridge in south-western Australia,
                 appear well suited to large-volume CO2 storage (Olierook et al., 2013; Urosevic et al., 2018). A
                 comparatively low natural pore pressure, resulting from limited formation fluid, is one of the key indicators
                 used to screen candidate CO2-storage reservoirs (Harpalani et al., 2006; Abdulkarem et al., 2012; Liu et al.,
                 2015). As injection proceeds, however, rising pore pressure shifts the effective stress state of the formation,
                 raising the chance of fault reactivation and/or seal leakage near the reservoir. CO2 volumes therefore need
                 to be kept below the level that would push pore pressure past the threshold at which faults reactivate or the
                 seal leaks. Defining that critical pore-pressure threshold gives the storage reservoir a margin of safety that
                 helps manage these risks (Mazumder et al., 2006; Anggara et al., 2016; Sampath et al., 2020). Coal seams
                 represent another potential storage target with distinct injectivity and containment behaviour, as reviewed
                 by Hosseinzadeh et al. (2024a).
                    Site characterisation is the first stage of any CO2-injection project (Doughty et al., 2008; Dai et al., 2014;
                 Harp et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2010; Birkholzer et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2020). Geomechanical modelling
                 offers an early, practical way to gauge whether a candidate reservoir is suitable, revealing the mechanical
                 characteristics of the reservoir and its cap rock and flagging any susceptibility to fracturing. Quantified
                 model outputs support the long-term safety case for injection by indicating where and what type of pore-
                 pressure monitoring is needed, and by giving a systematic basis for accountability over the life of the project
                 (Al-Ameri et al., 2016; Lyu et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2021). This information, together with ongoing formation
                 monitoring, can also help improve the technical and economic performance of the reservoir over time. A
                 recent review by Khan et al. (2024) brings together the numerical approaches used across the field for
                 modelling reservoir pressure, ground uplift, caprock fault reactivation, and CO2 leakage, together with the
                 monitoring techniques used to verify stored CO2. Complementary approaches that infer reservoir pressure
                 directly from surface deformation data offer a lower-cost alternative to dense subsurface instrumentation
                 for this kind of monitoring (Abdollahi et al., 2024).
                    A clear picture of reservoir–seal efficiency, and of how durable that seal remains as formation pressure
                 climbs, is needed to demonstrate transparently and accountably that CO2 injection can continue safely
                 without leakage (Frash et al., 2017; Palusznet al., 2020). An integrated geomechanical modelling workflow,
                 drawing together detailed reservoir geology, the in-situ stress regime, rock mechanical properties and pore-
                 pressure data, gives a fuller picture of how the reservoir will behave as stress conditions evolve. Such

                 hydrogen storage and production (Hosseinzadeh et al., 2025b). More recently, machine-learning surrogates
                 trained on Mohr-Coulomb-based geomechanical criteria have been proposed as a faster alternative to full
                 numerical simulation for forecasting fault-reactivation risk during CO2 storage (de Lima et al., 2026).
                    This study develops a 3D coupled reservoir geomechanical model to evaluate reservoir–seal integrity
                 for the proposed storage of CO2 in the Harvey Ridge reservoir, Western Australia. The model draws on a
                 wide range of compiled data, including reservoir geology, geomechanical parameters, mapped faults and
                 fractures, petrophysical well logs, interpreted water saturation, and reservoir pressures taken from a dynamic
                 simulation model, with seismic inversion providing a further route to constraining reservoir elastic and
                 petrophysical properties (Hosseinzadeh et al., 2025a). Initial pore-pressure distribution is calculated using
                 the corrected Eaton (1975) equation, while in-situ stress values are derived through a poroelastic approach
                 and calibrated against leak-off test (LOT) and extended leak-off test (XLOT) data. Borehole image (BHI)
                 log interpretation is used to establish the prevailing horizontal in-situ stress directions in the reservoir, and
                 because the reservoir's stress state shifts as CO2 is injected, a pore-pressure–stress coupling approach is
                 applied across the different injection phases considered (Vidal et al., 2009; Kim and Hosseini., 2014; Khan
                 et al., 2018; Konstantinovskaya et al., 2020; Jung et al., 2020). Once built and calibrated, the 3D MEM is
                 coupled with pressure and water-saturation data to yield outputs that indicate how well the existing fault
                 system will hold and how susceptible it is to reactivation as pore pressure rises.

                 Geological setting
                 Tectonics
                 The Perth Basin is a north-south-trending regional extensional feature that lies along the margin of Western
                 Australia's coastline. It formed through Permian–Cretaceous tectonic activity linked to the separation of
                 Australia from India (Harris., 1994; Mory et al., 2005; Dillinger and Esteban., 2014). A Permian–Triassic
                 extension event drove the complex rifting seen in the area and produced substantial clastic sediment
                 deposits during that time. Extension continued into the Jurassic, accompanied by the development of graben
                 structures that were infilled mainly with marine sediments. This rift system later contributed to the break-
                 up of the Gondwana supercontinent, generating dextral trans-tensional stresses across the basin's northwest
                 during the Late Cretaceous and producing widespread tectonic deformation ranging from reverse and strike-
                 slip faulting to volcanism and erosion (Plumb, 1979; Song and Cawood, 2000; Borissova et al., 2014; Hall
                 et al., 2017; Olierook et al., 2019).
                    To the east, the basin is bounded by the Yilgarn Craton and the north-south-trending Darling Fault, while
                 to the west it extends offshore towards the coastal margin. Listric faults trending north-northwest dominate
                 the basin and governed sediment deposition, which broadly kept pace with the accommodation space created
                 by rift-related faulting and subsidence (Lambeck., 1987; Whittaker et al., 2013; Olierook et al., 2015; Cai
                 et al., 2017).

                 Methodology and available data
                 Establishing Harvey Field geomechanical parameters
                 Determining geomechanical parameters accurately is central to any quantitative geomechanical study, and
                 laboratory analysis of core data offers a reliable way of obtaining these properties (Dewhurst and Hennig.,
                 2003; Lijith et al., 2019; Kolawole and Ispas., 2020). Well logs, by contrast, are recorded far more widely
                 and give continuous coverage across formations, whereas core data is available only at limited depths. It
                 therefore matters to establish, wherever feasible, a relationship linking well-log responses to core-derived
                 geomechanical parameters, since such relationships allow those parameters to be extrapolated across whole
                 wellbore sections where core is unavailable. In this study, the limited rock-mechanical data obtained from
                 core specimens at several depths were used in this way to calibrate the well-log-derived geomechanical
                 properties.

                 Coupled Geomechanical Modeling
                 A variety of techniques exist for coupling reservoir dynamic data with geomechanical models (Settari
                 and Walter., 2001; Xiong et al., 2013; Zhang and Mack., 2017; McMillan et al., 2019; Jamaloei., 2021;
                 Hawes et al., 2021), and these coupled models are useful for revealing stress-related reservoir behaviour.
                 Fully coupled methods can resolve the complete set of geomechanical equations while accounting for
                 hydromechanical interactions, but doing so generally forces some simplification of the hydraulic or
                 geomechanical formulations compared with standalone, uncoupled reservoir and geomechanical models.
                    An alternative is a partly coupled method, built by linking standard reservoir and geomechanical
                 simulators, in which the stress and fluid-flow equations are solved separately at each phase and data is
                 passed back and forth between the two simulators. This tends to be a flexible approach that runs quickly in
                 CPU terms and can readily absorb new mathematical developments as they emerge, in either the reservoir or
                 the geomechanical simulation. The partial coupling involves several exchange steps; if each step is carried
                 out only once, the coupling is termed ‘explicit’, whereas if it is repeated until the stress distributions and
                 fluid flows for a given pore volume converge, it is termed "iterative".
                    Coupling the pore-pressure history from a dynamic reservoir simulator with the reservoir's
                 geomechanical parameters produces what is termed a one-way partially coupled model: pore pressures
                 from the reservoir simulation are passed through poroelastic relationships to derive stress distributions
                 and deformation. This kind of partial coupling is an effective way to preserve the reservoir's distinct
                 geomechanical characteristics (Settari and Walters, 2001).
                    This study centres on how CO2 injection affects the reservoir and its cap rock. Where the pore-pressure
                 profile stays comparatively low, deformation is unlikely to noticeably alter reservoir properties such as
                 porosity, so a coupled geomechanical model is generally unnecessary. Because CCS reservoirs receive CO2
                 in multiple stages, however, it is worth applying a one-way coupling approach to gauge how susceptible the
                 existing faults are to reactivation as injection continues over time. Thermal effects arising from injecting
                 cool CO2 into the warmer reservoir have been left out of this study. This omission is deliberate rather than
                 incidental. The pore-pressure and saturation histories used to drive the geomechanical model were produced
                 by an isothermal dynamic simulation, so no reservoir temperature field was available to impose as a thermal
                 load, and because the Harvey site is still pre-injection, the injection temperature, the rate-dependent Joule-
                 Thomson cooling and the extent of the resulting near-well cooling front would all have to be assumed rather
                 than measured. Cooling of this kind contracts the rock skeleton and reduces the effective horizontal stresses
                 within the cooled volume, which lowers the margin against tensile and shear failure close to the injectors
                 and at the base of the seal (Gor et al., 2013; Selvadurai and Suvorov, 2016; Mathur et al., 2024). That
                 volume is confined to the immediate vicinity of the injection wells, however, whereas the faults assessed
                 here lie several hundred metres to kilometres away, where the stress perturbation is governed by pore-
                 pressure change rather than by temperature. The isothermal treatment is therefore considered adequate for
                 the field-scale fault-reactivation question addressed in this paper, and the results reported below should be
                 read as the pressure-driven response; a fully coupled thermo-hydro-mechanical analysis is required before
                 any statement can be made about near-wellbore and near-seal integrity within the cooled region, and forms
                 the subject of ongoing work.

                 Result and Discussion
                 3D Mechanical Earth Model (MEM)
                 Building an MEM makes fuller use of the available geomechanical data, mapping the formations'
                 mechanical properties across the whole study area. A properly calibrated MEM can then be used to identify
                 the most suitable approaches for safe CO2 injection and field development, with the 3D modelling outputs
                 providing field-wide property distributions drawn from combined seismic and well data.
                 Geometry. Defining the reservoir boundary conditions is typically the most time-consuming part of
                 building a geomechanical FEM model. Formation surfaces and fault polygons are usually derived from
                 seismic interpretation, which is well suited to constraining stratigraphic and structural models for the area
                 of interest, and an upscaled geological grid can usefully be carried into the geomechanical model. Even
                 so, the FE grid still has to satisfy certain requirements, most importantly that it fully covers the reservoir
                 boundaries (Fig. 7). Sideburdens — limiting boundaries built parallel to the reservoir grid direction — were
                 added around the studied area, with a lithostatic load representing the sedimentary overburden applied as
                 the top boundary condition; the cap rock is treated as part of the overburden and so is excluded from the
                 modelled volume. The underburden was extended below the constructed grids to improve the model's aspect
                 ratio and give a more realistic transfer of stress from the boundaries into the reservoir and overburden during
                 stress modelling.

                 Conclusions
                 Bringing together static geological, dynamic reservoir and geomechanical models within a 4D finite-element
                 framework gives a meaningful picture of the stress state of the South-West Hub (SWH) Carbon Capture and
                 Storage (CCS) reservoir in Western Australia, based on data from the Harvey wellbore. Multiple 1D and
                 3D iterations were carried out during modelling to calibrate the Sh/SH values, validate the wellbore data
                 and account for fault activation within the reservoir formation.
                    The model estimated Sv to range between 17 and 60 MPa, SH between 22 and 75 MPa, and Sh between 21
                 and 72 MPa. More than thirty faults were mapped across the field, predominantly trending N-S, consistent
                 with the dominant regional fault orientation.
                    After optimising the coupled model, the reservoir's in-situ stress system was modelled in stages through
                 a series of optimisation runs. Overall, the results point to no significant risk of strain or fault failure in the
                 Harvey reservoir under the predicted pressure changes.
                    The area representing principal stress tends to grow as pore pressure rises, potentially reaching the rock
                 failure envelope and increasing the chance of formation failure, including fault reactivation. Nonetheless,
                 the Mohr-circle results from the model simulation show no possibility of failure occurring in either the
                 Yalgorup or Wonnerup formations, at any timestep through to 2050 and at any modelled cell location. The
                 fault yield mode parameters generated at each modelled timestep likewise showed no failure anywhere in
                 the reservoir section of the Harvey field.
                    These conclusions apply to the isothermal, pressure-driven response of the reservoir. Thermal stresses
                 generated by injecting CO2 at a temperature below that of the formation are not represented in the model,
                 and such stresses can be significant close to the injection wells and at the base of the seal. The finding that no
                 fault reactivation is expected is therefore robust at the field scale, where pore-pressure change dominates the
